Intellectual Property Legislations relate to creations of the human intellect, including ideas, inventions, innovations, creative expressions, research outcomes, and technological developments. The legal rights granted in respect of such creations are collectively known as Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs). In an increasingly globalised economy characterised by cross-border trade and competition, the protection of intellectual property has become essential for encouraging innovation and creativity.

By granting statutory rights to creators and inventors, intellectual property laws ensure that individuals and organisations receive fair economic returns for their intellectual efforts. These rights enable creators to commercially exploit their work while preventing unauthorised use or imitation by others. Intellectual Property Rights broadly cover the following two areas:

Indian Copyright Act: This legislation protects the rights of authors and creators of original literary and artistic works. These include books, writings, musical compositions, paintings, sculptures, films, and computer programs. The Act also extends protection to performers such as actors, singers, and musicians, as well as to producers of sound recordings and broadcasting organisations. Copyright protection encourages creative expression by granting exclusive rights over reproduction, distribution, and communication of protected works.

Industrial Property Rights: Industrial property rights safeguard inventions and distinctive features that provide commercial identity to goods or services. These include patents, trademarks, industrial designs, and trade secrets. Such rights protect technological innovations, original product designs, and distinctive signs that differentiate one enterprise from another in the marketplace. By protecting industrial property, the law promotes research, innovation, and fair competition, while preventing misuse of proprietary knowledge.
Miscellaneous Laws: The Information Technology Act, 2000

The Information Technology Act, 2000 addresses legal issues arising from electronic communication and digital transactions. With the expansion of online business, electronic contracts, and digital data exchange, it became necessary to establish a legal framework governing electronic dealings. The Act grants legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures, thereby validating online transactions and communications.
Miscellaneous Laws: The Information Technology Act, 2000

The Act also provides that electronic records and communications are admissible as evidence, ensuring legal certainty in digital business operations. Additionally, it deals with cyber offences such as hacking, unauthorised access to computer systems, deliberate spread of computer viruses, and transmission of obscene material in electronic form. Such acts are classified as criminal offences, reflecting the law’s role in promoting cybersecurity and trust in digital commerce.
Miscellaneous Laws: The Information Technology Act, 2000

Since all business, trade, and commercial activities must operate within the statutory framework of the country, it is essential for enterprises to consider relevant business laws while defining their objectives, strategies, and operational policies. Awareness and understanding of these laws enable businesses to identify their legal rights and obligations, anticipate regulatory challenges, and adopt compliant and ethical practices. Ultimately, legal literacy supports informed decision-making and contributes to long-term organisational sustainability.

modules.title: Introduction
text: Business depends on being able to buy and sell goods with certainty. In India, the law on the sale of movable goods is in the Sale of Goods Act, 1930. Before this Act, the law of sale of goods was inside Chapter VII of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. As business became more complex, a separate and complete law was needed. The Sale of Goods Act came into force on 1 July 1930. The Act has 66 sections in seven parts.
It covers: forming a contract of sale, rights and duties of buyers and sellers, when ownership (property) passes from seller to buyer, performing the contract, remedies for breach, and auction sales.

It applies only to movable goods. It does not apply to immovable property (such as land and buildings), which is governed by the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Every business that buys raw materials, sells finished goods or makes distribution arrangements is governed by this Act.
The Act has not been fully amended since it was made. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and the Indian Contract Act, 1872 work alongside it for disputes and contract duties from sales.

modules.title: Contract of Sale
text: 2.1 Meaning and definition (Section 4(1)) A contract of sale of goods is a contract in which the seller transfers, or agrees to transfer, the property in goods to the buyer for a price.
"Property in goods" means ownership of the goods, not just physical possession. The seller can be an individual, a firm, a company, or any person legally able to make a contract.
There must be a transfer, or an agreement to transfer.
The subject matter must be goods.

The payment must be a price in money. If payment is partly in money and partly in goods, it can still be a contract of sale, as long as there is a money part. A pure exchange of goods for goods is barter. The Act does not cover barter. 2.2 Contract of sale as a specific contract A contract of sale is a type of contract under the Indian Contract Act, 1872. So all the needs of a valid contract must be met: offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity, free consent, legality of object and certainty of terms. The Sale of Goods Act gives special rules that add to the general law and, where they differ, override it, for sales of goods. Section 5: a contract of sale can be in writing, by word of mouth, or implied from the conduct of the parties. No particular form is needed. For immovable property, the Registration Act, 1908 needs registration. Since this Act deals only with movable goods, such formalities are generally not needed. 2.3 Subject matter: goods Section 2(7): goods means every kind of movable property other than actionable claims and money. Goods include stocks, shares, growing crops, grass, and things attached to or part of land that are agreed to be cut off (severed) before sale or under the contract. Intellectual property rights (like patents and copyrights), when in a physical form, may be treated as goods. Not goods: money in current use as legal tender and actionable claims such as debts.
Existing goods (Section 2(6)) = goods owned or possessed by the seller at the time of the contract.

Future goods = goods the seller will make, produce or get after the contract. Section 6: a contract to sell future goods is an agreement to sell, not a completed sale, because the goods do not yet exist or the seller does not yet have them.

Specific goods = goods identified and agreed upon at the time of the contract. Ascertained goods = goods that are not specific at the time of the contract but later become identified and separated from other goods of the same kind. Unascertained goods = goods described only by description, with no specific identification at the time of the contract.

2.4 Price Section 2(10): price is the money consideration for a sale of goods. Section 9: the price may be fixed by the contract, left to be fixed in a way agreed by the parties, or decided by the course of dealing between the parties. If it is not decided in any of these ways, Section 9(2): the buyer must pay a reasonable price. What is reasonable is a question of fact in each case. Section 10: if the price is to be fixed by a third-party valuer and the valuer cannot or does not value, the contract is void.
If goods were delivered under such a contract and one party's fault stopped the valuation, that party must pay damages to the other.

modules.title: Essentials of a Contract of Sale
text: Two parties A buyer (Section 2(1): a person who buys or agrees to buy goods) and a seller (Section 2(13): a person who sells or agrees to sell goods). A contract needs at least two parties, so a person cannot ordinarily sell goods to themselves. But a co-owner may sell their undivided share to another co-owner. This is a valid contract of sale.

Transfer of property The main purpose is transfer of ownership from seller to buyer. This makes it different from hire, pledge or bailment, where possession may pass but ownership does not. Sections 18 to 25 decide when property passes. This matters, especially for who bears the risk of loss or damage.

Goods as subject matter Only movable goods are covered. Immovable property is outside the Act. Goods may be existing, or future goods yet to be made, produced or acquired. A contract for goods that are part of a larger mass (an undivided share) is also recognised.

Price in money The payment must include a money element. A pure swap of one commodity for another is barter, not sale. If it is part money, part goods, courts generally accept it as a sale, if the money part is real and not just nominal. The consideration need not be adequate but must be real.

Capacity of parties Anyone competent to contract under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 can make a contract of sale. Section 11 of the Contract Act: a party must be of age of majority, of sound mind, and not disqualified by law. A contract of sale with a minor is void. If a seller is an undischarged insolvent, the contract may be challenged, depending on the goods and the availability of the Official Assignee.

Free consent Consent must be free. If it is got by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake, the contract is voidable (can be cancelled) at the option of the party whose consent was not free (Sections 14 to 22 of the Contract Act). Example: a seller fraudulently misrepresents the quality or nature of goods to make the buyer buy.

Legality of object and consideration The object and the payment must be lawful. A contract to sell prohibited goods, stolen goods, or goods whose trade is banned is void from the start (void ab initio). Selling goods against licensing rules (example: scheduled drugs without authorisation) is void for illegality.

Formalities No particular form is needed: it may be oral, written or implied from conduct. Section 5(2) (as the PDF states): where the goods are above a value set under local laws (for example, certain state enactments), a written and stamped contract may be required. In practice, business contracts are written to avoid disputes about terms. Check yourself (Part 3)

modules.title: Sale and Agreement to Sell
text: This is one of the most important ideas in the Act. The two differ in when ownership passes, who bears the loss, and what remedies the parties have.

Sale: a contract in which ownership passes from seller to buyer immediately, at the time of the contract. From that moment the buyer is the owner and bears the risk of later loss or damage, even if goods have not yet been delivered. Agreement to sell: a contract in which the transfer of ownership is to take place at a future time or when certain conditions are met. Until then, ownership stays with the seller, and the seller bears the risk of loss. An agreement to sell becomes a sale when the time passes or the conditions are fulfilled.
Transfer of ownership - Sale: Immediate: passes when the contract is made; Agreement to Sell: Future: passes when conditions are fulfilled.
Nature - Sale: Executed contract; Agreement to Sell: Executory contract.
Risk of loss - Sale: Buyer bears the risk; Agreement to Sell: Seller continues to bear the risk.
Remedy for breach - Sale: Real right: buyer may sue for the goods; Agreement to Sell: Personal right: only a suit for damages.
Insolvency of buyer - Sale: Seller must deliver and claim the price as a preferred creditor; Agreement to Sell: Seller may refuse to deliver and keeps the goods.
Insolvency of seller - Sale: Buyer can claim the goods from the Official Receiver; Agreement to Sell: Buyer can only claim a rateable dividend, not the goods.

A contract of sale may be made in writing, orally, partly in writing and partly oral, or implied from conduct. It may provide for immediate delivery or payment, delivery or payment in instalments, or delay of both to a future date.

For example, Rajan, a grain merchant in Amritsar, agrees to sell 200 bags of wheat to Sunil, a flour mill owner in Ludhiana, at ₹2,200 per bag. The bags are identified, weighed and handed over to Sunil's truck immediately after signing. This is a sale: ownership passes at once.

For example, if Rajan instead agrees to supply 200 bags of the next harvest (not yet existing) after three months, this is an agreement to sell. Ownership passes only when the goods are identified, weighed and appropriated to the contract after the harvest.

modules.title: Conditions and Warranties
text: 5.1 Meaning of condition (Section 12(2)) A condition is a stipulation (term) essential to the main purpose of the contract. Its breach gives the right to treat the contract as repudiated (cancelled). A condition goes to the root of the contract.

On breach of condition, the buyer may reject the goods, treat the contract as ended, and claim damages. So a condition is more important than a warranty. Example: a buyer buys a machine for a particular purpose and tells the seller that purpose. The seller's promise that it is fit for that purpose is a condition. If it is unfit, the buyer may reject it completely.
5.2 Meaning of warranty (Section 12(3)) A warranty is a stipulation collateral (secondary) to the main purpose of the contract.
Its breach gives a claim for damages only. The buyer cannot reject the goods and cancel the contract.
If the buyer accepts goods in breach of warranty, they cannot reject them later. The remedy is the difference in value between the goods delivered and the goods as warranted.
5.3 When a condition is treated as a warranty (Section 13) In some cases a buyer who could cancel the contract for breach of condition may choose (or be made) to treat it as a breach of warranty.
The buyer voluntarily waives the condition or chooses to treat the breach of condition as a breach of warranty.
The contract is non-severable and the buyer has accepted the goods or part of them.

The contract is for specific goods and property has passed to the buyer. Practical meaning: once property in specific goods has passed and the buyer has accepted the goods, the buyer loses the right to reject them, even for breach of condition. The only remedy is damages. Note: the third circumstance is not written as a separate clause in Section 13. It comes from reading Section 13 with Section 62 (which keeps the parties' right to waive conditions) and from court decisions. So it is doctrinal (based on principle), not directly listed. In another place the PDF gives the third circumstance as "where fulfilment of the condition is excused by law due to impossibility or otherwise.".
Importance - Condition: Essential to the main purpose; Warranty: Collateral to the main purpose.
Breach consequences - Condition: Repudiate contract + claim damages; Warranty: Claim damages only.
Treatment - Condition: May be treated as a warranty at the buyer's option; Warranty: Cannot be raised to a condition.
Effect on contract - Condition: Entitles rejection of goods; Warranty: Does not entitle rejection.
5.4 Implied conditions Implied means not written, but added by law into every contract of sale, unless the parties clearly exclude them.

Condition as to title (Section 14(a)) In a sale, the seller has the right to sell the goods. In an agreement to sell, the seller will have the right to sell when property is to pass. This is the most basic implied condition. A seller without good title cannot pass title.

Condition as to description (Section 15) In a sale by description, the goods must match the description. If goods are sold by both description and sample, it is not enough that the bulk matches the sample. It must also match the description. This applies whether or not the buyer has seen the goods.

Condition as to fitness for purpose (Section 16(1)) The buyer tells the seller the particular purpose (clearly or by implication), so as to show the buyer relies on the seller's skill or judgement, and the goods are of a kind the seller normally supplies. Then the goods must be reasonably fit for that purpose. This does not apply if the buyer buys under a patent or trade name.

Condition as to merchantable quality (Section 16(2)) Goods bought by description from a seller who deals in goods of that description (a manufacturer or not) must be of merchantable quality. The Act does not define it. Courts say it means the goods are such that a buyer who knows their condition would buy them without asking for a lower price. Damaged, defective or unsuitable for ordinary use goods may fail this condition.

Condition in sales by sample (Section 17) Three implied conditions: (i) the bulk matches the sample in quality; (ii) the buyer has a reasonable chance to compare bulk with sample; (iii) the goods are free from any hidden defect that makes them unmerchantable and would not be seen on reasonable examination of the sample. 5.5 Implied warranties These are minimum protections for the buyer, whatever the parties agreed. Warranty of quiet possession (Section 14(b)): the buyer will have and enjoy quiet possession of the goods. If a third party with a better title disturbs the buyer's possession, the buyer can claim damages from the seller. Warranty of freedom from encumbrances (Section 14(c)): the goods are free from any charge or claim of a third party that was not declared or known to the buyer at the time of the contract. If the buyer later has to pay such a third-party claim, the buyer can recover the cost from the seller. Check yourself (Part 5)

modules.title: Passing of Property in Goods
text: Passing of property means the transfer of ownership from seller to buyer. It is different from possession: a buyer may have the goods without being the owner, and ownership may pass even before physical delivery. It is important because risk, remedies and rights over the goods generally depend on ownership.

The main rules are in Sections 18 to 25. The rules Section 18 (unascertained goods): property cannot pass until the goods are ascertained. Example: a seller agrees to sell 50 bags of wheat out of a stock of 500 bags. Ownership does not pass until 50 specific bags are identified and set apart for the buyer.

Section 19 (specific or ascertained goods): property passes when the parties intend it to pass. The intention can be found from the terms of the contract, the conduct of the parties and the circumstances. If the contract is not clear, Sections 20 to 24 give rules.
If the goods are in a deliverable state and the contract is unconditional, property normally passes when the contract is made.
If the seller must do something to make the goods deliverable, or must weigh, measure or test them to fix the price, property passes only after that act is done and the buyer has notice.
Unascertained or future goods: property passes when goods of the contract description are unconditionally appropriated to the contract with the assent (agreement) of the other party.
Goods on approval or sale-or-return: property passes when the buyer accepts the goods, adopts the transaction, or keeps the goods beyond the agreed or reasonable time without rejecting them.
Section 26 (risk): risk ordinarily follows property. Goods stay at the seller's risk until ownership passes. After that they are generally at the buyer's risk, unless the parties agree otherwise.

modules.title: Transfer of Title by Non-Owners
text: General rule: nemo dat quod non habet = "no one can give what they do not have." Section 27: if goods are sold by a person who is not the owner and who does not sell with the owner's authority or consent, the buyer does not get a better title than the seller had.
Example: if stolen goods are sold to an innocent buyer, the buyer does not get valid title, because the thief had no ownership to pass.
This rule protects the true owner. But it can hurt innocent buyers who buy in good faith. So the Act has exceptions where a non-owner can pass valid title.

Mercantile agent: a mercantile agent in possession of goods or documents of title with the owner's consent may pass valid title if the buyer acts in good faith and without notice that the agent lacked authority.
Section 28 (joint owners): one of several joint owners in sole possession of goods may pass valid title to a good-faith buyer.
Section 29 (voidable contract): a person who got goods under a voidable contract may pass valid title before the contract is cancelled, if the buyer acts in good faith and without notice.
Section 30(1) (seller in possession after sale): a seller who stays in possession after the sale may pass valid title to a second buyer acting in good faith.

Section 30(2) (buyer in possession): a buyer who has the goods before full ownership has passed may pass valid title to a good-faith purchaser. In short: the nemo dat rule protects ownership; the exceptions build business confidence and protect honest buyers. Check yourself (Parts 6 and 7)

modules.title: Performance of the Contract of Sale
text: The seller's duty is to deliver the goods. The buyer's duty is to accept and pay for them, as the contract says.
Delivery and payment are concurrent (happen together) unless agreed otherwise. Neither party must perform before the other has performed or offered to perform.
Section 2(2): delivery is the voluntary transfer of possession from one person to another.
Three modes: Actual delivery: goods are physically handed over to the buyer or the buyer's agent.
Constructive delivery: a third party holding the goods acknowledges to the buyer that they hold them on the buyer's behalf. Example: a warehousekeeper who attorns (acknowledges) to the buyer.
Symbolic delivery: transfer of something that represents the goods, such as keys of a warehouse or a bill of lading.
Section 33: delivery can be made by doing anything the parties agree to treat as delivery, or anything that puts the goods in the possession of the buyer or their agent.
If no place is agreed, delivery is at the seller's place of business (or residence if there is no business address).
If the seller must send the goods, they must send within a reasonable time. Unless agreed otherwise, the seller bears the expenses of putting the goods into a deliverable state.
Delivery of part of the goods is not delivery of the whole.
Less than contracted: the buyer may reject the goods.
More than contracted: the buyer may accept the contracted quantity and reject the rest, or reject the whole.
Mixed with goods of a different description: the buyer may accept the contracted goods and reject the rest, or reject the whole lot.

Unless agreed otherwise, the buyer is not bound to accept delivery in instalments. If the contract expressly provides for instalments paid for separately, the buyer's right to cancel the contract after the seller's breach in one instalment depends on whether the breach is fundamental to the whole contract or severable.

The buyer is deemed to have accepted the goods when: the buyer tells the seller they accept; or the goods are delivered and the buyer does any act inconsistent with the seller's ownership; or the buyer keeps the goods without giving notice of rejection after a reasonable time.
Once goods are accepted, the buyer loses the right to reject them for breach of condition.

If goods are delivered that the buyer has not examined before, the buyer is not deemed to have accepted them until the buyer has had a reasonable opportunity to examine them and see if they match the contract.
The seller must, on request, give a reasonable opportunity to examine.

modules.title: Duties and Rights of the Parties
text: A contract of sale creates mutual duties. The seller must deliver goods that match the contract. The buyer must accept the goods and pay the price (Section 31). These duties and rights are reciprocal (each depends on the other).
Deliver the goods as agreed. Example: a wholesaler agrees to deliver 200 cartons of packaged food to a retailer's warehouse by a date.

Deliver goods according to the contract: they must match the description, sample, quality, quantity and other terms. Example: if cotton fabric of a specified grade is ordered, the seller cannot deliver a lower grade. Non-matching goods may give the buyer the right to reject or claim damages.

Deliver at the agreed time and place. If no place is fixed, delivery is generally at the seller's place of business or residence. If the seller must send the goods, they must be sent within a reasonable time.

Put goods into a deliverable state: goods are in a deliverable state when the buyer is bound to take delivery. Example: machinery sold on condition that it will be packed, tested and prepared for transport.
Deliver the correct quantity (Section 37). Example: a buyer orders 500 units and the seller delivers 400. The buyer may reject the delivery, or accept the 400 and pay at the contract rate.

Allow examination of goods: give a reasonable opportunity to inspect. Example: a buyer of electronic components should be able to check model numbers, quantity and visible defects. 9.2 Rights of the seller.
Right to receive the price. If property has passed and the buyer wrongfully refuses to pay, the seller may sue for the price (Section 55).

Right to refuse delivery if payment is not made. Unless the contract allows credit, payment and delivery are concurrent. If the buyer refuses to pay when payment is due, the seller may refuse to deliver.
Rights of an unpaid seller (Section 45). A seller who has not received the whole price is an unpaid seller. The seller may have rights against the goods: lien, stoppage in transit and resale.
Right to claim damages for non-acceptance (Section 56). Example: a manufacturer makes goods to the buyer's order and the buyer refuses delivery without lawful reason.

Right to claim charges for care and custody (Section 44). If the buyer neglects or refuses to take delivery within a reasonable time, the seller may claim compensation for loss and a reasonable charge for care and custody of the goods.
Overview of the unpaid seller's rights (Section 45)
Right of lien = right to keep the goods until payment.
Overview of the unpaid seller's rights (Section 45)
Right of stoppage in transit = right to recall goods in transit if the buyer becomes insolvent.
Overview of the unpaid seller's rights (Section 45)

Right of resale = right to resell in suitable cases and recover any loss. These are in addition to personal remedies: a suit for the price (Section 55) and a suit for damages for non-acceptance (Section 56). 9.3 Duties of the buyer.
Overview of the unpaid seller's rights (Section 45)
Accept delivery of goods that match the contract. Example: 100 office chairs of a specified model are delivered exactly as ordered. Refusing them may be a breach.
Overview of the unpaid seller's rights (Section 45)
Pay the price as agreed. If no payment time is fixed, payment and delivery are usually concurrent. In a credit sale, pay within the credit period.
Overview of the unpaid seller's rights (Section 45)

Apply for delivery where required (Section 35): unless agreed otherwise, the seller is not bound to deliver until the buyer asks for delivery. Example: goods lying in the seller's warehouse that the buyer must collect.
Overview of the unpaid seller's rights (Section 45)
Take delivery within a reasonable time. If the buyer delays without good reason, the seller may suffer storage costs or goods may spoil, and the buyer may be liable under Section 44.
Overview of the unpaid seller's rights (Section 45)

Not wrongfully reject goods. The buyer may reject only on a lawful ground: breach of condition, wrong description, wrong quantity or non-conformity. Rejecting goods that match the contract is wrongful, and the seller may claim damages. 9.4 Rights of the buyer.
Overview of the unpaid seller's rights (Section 45)
Right to receive delivery. If the seller wrongfully neglects or refuses to deliver, the buyer may sue for damages for non-delivery (Section 57).
Overview of the unpaid seller's rights (Section 45)
Right to examine goods before acceptance (Section 41).
Overview of the unpaid seller's rights (Section 45)
Right to reject non-conforming goods, subject to the rules on conditions, warranties and acceptance. Example: stainless steel utensils ordered but aluminium utensils delivered.
Overview of the unpaid seller's rights (Section 45)
Right to claim damages. For breach of warranty the buyer cannot reject the goods on that ground alone, but may claim damages under Section 59.
Overview of the unpaid seller's rights (Section 45)

Right to specific performance (Section 58). For specific or ascertained goods, where damages are not enough, the buyer may ask the court to order that the contract be performed. This is discretionary (the court decides) and may be granted where goods are unique or not easily available in the market.

modules.title: Breach of Contract of Sale
text: Breach happens when a party fails to perform their duties. Examples: non-delivery, delivery of defective or non-matching goods, non-payment, refusal to accept delivery, or repudiation (refusing) before performance is due. The Act gives special remedies, in addition to the general remedies under the Indian Contract Act, 1872.

Suit for non-delivery (Section 57) If the seller wrongfully neglects or refuses to deliver, the buyer may sue for damages for non-delivery. The damages are the estimated loss directly and naturally resulting from the breach in the ordinary course of events. This equals the difference between the contract price and the market (current) price on the date of breach.

Suit for specific performance (Section 58) In a suit for breach of a contract to deliver specific or ascertained goods, the court may, if it thinks fit, order that the contract be performed specifically, without giving the defendant the option of keeping the goods by paying damages. It is discretionary and usually used where goods are unique or have special qualities that money cannot properly pay for.

Suit for breach of warranty (Section 59) For breach of warranty (or where the buyer chooses or is forced to treat a breach of condition as a breach of warranty), the buyer cannot reject the goods on that account alone. The buyer may sue for damages and may set up the breach in reduction or cancellation of the price. Measure of damages: the estimated loss directly and naturally resulting from the breach. For breach of warranty of quality, this is prima facie (at first view) the difference between the value of the goods at delivery and the value they would have had if they matched the warranty.

Anticipatory breach (repudiation before the due date) If a party repudiates before the date of performance, the other party may accept the repudiation and sue for damages at once, or wait until the date fixed for performance and then sue.

Suit for recovery of price (Section 55) If property has passed to the buyer and the buyer wrongfully neglects or refuses to pay, the seller may sue for the price. If the price is payable on a fixed day, whether or not delivery is made, and the buyer wrongfully refuses to pay, the seller may recover the price even if property has not passed and even if the goods have not been appropriated to the contract. Check yourself (Part 10)

modules.title: Auction Sale
text: An auction is a public sale where goods are offered to many possible buyers and sold to the highest bidder.
The rules are in Section 64 of the Act.
The auctioneer is the agent of the seller for the auction. The auctioneer is not the buyer's agent, unless there is a special custom or agreement.
Completion of sale: the sale is complete when the auctioneer announces it by the fall of the hammer or in another customary way. Until then, any bidder may withdraw a bid.

Reserve price and bidding for the seller: if the sale is subject to a right to bid on behalf of the seller, this right must be announced before the auction starts. If not, no seller or person acting for the seller may bid. The seller cannot make a fictitious bid. A sale against this rule may be treated as fraudulent by the buyer.

Knock-out agreements: a sale may be announced as subject to a reserved or upset price. Agreements between bidders not to outbid each other (knock-out agreements or bidder rings) are void under Section 64(5), because they are against public policy and defeat competitive bidding.

Right to bid expressly reserved: the seller may expressly reserve the right to bid. Then the seller, or one person acting as the seller's agent, may bid. It is not lawful to employ more than one person to bid without disclosing it. Example: at a machinery auction, the auctioneer calls for bids on a lathe machine and accepts a bid of two lakh rupees with the fall of the hammer. A binding contract is formed at that moment. The winning bidder cannot retract, and the seller cannot accept a higher bid from someone else. Check yourself (Part 11)

modules.title: Doctrine of Caveat Emptor
text: 12.1 Meaning and origin Caveat emptor is Latin for "let the buyer beware." It came from English common law and puts on the buyer the duty to be careful and examine goods before buying.

It reflects the laissez-faire (little interference) business thinking of the 19th century, when buyers and sellers were thought to deal at arm's length with equal information. It was brought into Indian sale of goods law and is codified in Section 16. Section 16 begins: "Subject to the provisions of this Act and of any other law for the time being in force, there is no implied warranty or condition as to the quality or fitness for any particular purpose of goods supplied under a contract of sale." So the seller is not normally required to tell the buyer about defects. It is the buyer's job to inspect, ask and be satisfied about quality, fitness and condition.
12.2 Application and effect Where caveat emptor applies, the buyer has no remedy for defects they could have found on ordinary examination before buying.

Example: a buyer buys a second-hand motor vehicle at an auction without inspecting it and later finds the engine is defective. If the defect was patent (discoverable on inspection), the buyer cannot claim against the seller. It works most strictly in auction sales and in sales by description where the buyer had a chance to examine the goods.

Fitness for a particular purpose (Section 16(1)): the buyer tells the seller the purpose, relies on the seller's skill or judgement, and the goods are of a kind the seller normally supplies. Then there is an implied condition of reasonable fitness.

Sale under a trade name (Section 16(1) proviso): even if goods are sold under a trade or patent name, the implied condition of fitness can still apply if the buyer shows they relied on the seller's skill or judgement and not only on the trade name.

Merchantable quality (Section 16(2)): goods bought by description from a seller who deals in such goods carry an implied condition of merchantable quality. The buyer keeps this protection even if goods are bought by description alone, without inspection.
Sale by sample (Section 17): implied conditions on quality and freedom from hidden (latent) defects override caveat emptor.

Fraud or misrepresentation: caveat emptor does not protect a seller who commits active fraud or material misrepresentation. If a false statement of fact makes the buyer buy, the buyer may cancel the contract or claim damages.

Usage of trade (Section 16(3)): an implied warranty or condition about quality or fitness may be added by trade usage. If a trade custom requires sellers to supply goods of a certain standard, that duty is an implied condition.

The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 has greatly changed caveat emptor. It gives consumers the right to protection against defective goods, the right to information, and the right to seek redress before consumer commissions. In business-to- consumer sales, sellers have duties that go well beyond the Sale of Goods Act. But in business-to-business deals, which are outside the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, caveat emptor continues to apply fully, subject only to the Section 16 exceptions. Business buyers are expected to do due diligence, negotiate warranties and add express contract protections.

modules.title: Definition of Partnership, Partner, and Firm
text: Governing Framework: The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 governs the formation, working, and dissolution of partnership firms in India.

Section 4 Definition: "Partnership is the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all." Four Essential Elements (Section 4)
Relationship between persons: At least two persons must join together.
Agreement to share profits: Partners agree to share the profits of the business (arises from contract, not status).
Business actually carried on: A lawful business must be carried on by all or any of them.
Mutual agency: Each partner acts for all—every partner is both a principal and an agent.
Meaning and Definition of Partnership: Scholar Views
Haney: Relation between persons competent to contract who agree to carry on a lawful business in common for private gain.
Meaning and Definition of Partnership: Scholar Views
William Spriegel: Each partner can bind the others, and personal assets of partners can be used to pay firm debts.
Meaning and Definition of Partnership: Scholar Views
Shelbina: Emphasised joint responsibility assumed through written or oral agreement.
Meaning and Definition of Partnership: Practical Example

Three software professionals—Arjun (client relations), Bhavna (development), and Chinmay (accounts)—agree to share profits equally from a web development business where each acts on behalf of the others. This satisfies all elements of Section 4.

Partner: Each individual person who has entered into a partnership agreement with one or more others. A partner is bound by the agreement and can act on behalf of the firm. Firm: The collective name for all persons who have entered into a partnership. The name under which they trade is called the Firm Name.
Key Legal Rule: A firm is NOT a separate legal entity (unlike a company). It has no legal existence apart from its partners, though it can sue and be sued in its firm name under procedural law.
Example: Kapoor and Mehta run 'K&M Traders'. They are the partners, 'K&M Traders' is the firm name, and together they are the firm. A creditor recovers debt from Kapoor and Mehta personally.
Determining the Existence of a Partnership
Sharing of profits is strong evidence of partnership, but NOT conclusive proof. Co-owners sharing property returns are not automatically partners.
Determining the Existence of a Partnership
Persons who receive a share of profits but are NOT partners: a. A lender of money to persons in business.
Determining the Existence of a Partnership
b. A previous owner receiving a share of profits as payment for selling goodwill. c. A servant or agent receiving profit-linked remuneration.
Determining the Existence of a Partnership
d. A widow or child of a deceased partner receiving a profit-linked annuity. Decisive Test: Mutual Agency—whether each person can bind the others through business acts done on behalf of the business.
Existence of Business: Must be a lawful commercial activity aimed at earning profit (not social or charitable).
Minimum & Maximum Persons: Minimum 2 persons; maximum generally limited to 50 under the Companies Act, 2013 and rules (traditionally 20 under earlier law).
Contractual Relationship: Arises from contract (oral or written), not status; partners must be competent to contract under the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
Sharing of Profits & Losses: Shared in the agreed ratio (losses follow the same ratio unless agreed otherwise).
Mutual Agency: Each partner is both principal and agent and can bind the firm in the ordinary course of business.
Utmost Good Faith: Fiduciary duty to act honestly, disclose material facts, and avoid conflicts of interest.
Unlimited Liability: Personal property of partners can be attached if firm assets cannot pay creditors.
Restriction on Transfer of Share: No partner can transfer their share to an outsider without unanimous consent of all partners.
Capital Contribution: Contributed in agreed proportions (need not be equal; a partner can even join without capital if others agree).
Duration: Continues at partners' pleasure (fixed term, specific venture, or at will); legally ends on death, insolvency, or retirement unless remaining partners agree to continue.
Ease of Formation — Simple oral or written agreement; registration is not compulsory (though advisable).: Unlimited Liability — Joint and several liability puts partners' personal assets at risk.
Pooling of Resources — Combines capital, skills, and networks of multiple people.: Uncertain Life — Death, insolvency, or retirement of a partner can dissolve the firm (subject to agreement).
Better Decision-Making — Multiple perspectives reduce impulsive or poor choices.: Risk of Conflict — Equal management rights can cause friction, delays, or deadlock.

Flexibility — Easy to change size, scope, or operations by mutual consent without legal procedures.: Limited Capital — Maximum partner cap (50) restricts raising huge capital for large-scale ventures.

Shared Risk — Losses are split across partners (e.g., Rs 15,000 loss split equally among 3 partners = Rs 5,000 each).: No Transferability of Share — Cannot sell share to an outsider without unanimous consent, creating illiquidity.

Protection of Interests & Specialisation — Each partner has a voice (and can dissolve if disagreeing), and partners can divide roles (finance, operations, client relations).: Scope — Best suited for small to medium enterprises built on mutual trust.

modules.title: Partnership Deed
text: A partnership deed is the written agreement containing all terms and conditions governing the relationship among partners. It is also called Articles of Partnership. No fixed format is legally prescribed, but if written, it must be properly stamped under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 and signed by all partners.
Unlike a company's Memorandum or Articles of Association, a partnership deed is NOT a public document.

modules.title: Kinds of Partnership
text: Partnerships are classified by duration (Partnership at Will vs Particular Partnership) and by liability (General Partnership vs Limited Partnership).

Partnership at Will (Section 7): No fixed term and not formed for a specific venture; continues as long as partners wish. Most common type in India. Dissolution Trigger: Active step required—any partner can dissolve it at any time by giving written notice to all other partners (e.g., Sharma sending written notice to Gupta after 3 years).

Particular Partnership (Section 8): Formed for a specific project/venture or for a fixed time period (common in construction, film production, event management, consulting). Dissolution Trigger: Automatic—dissolves automatically when the venture is completed or the fixed term expires, with no notice or agreement needed (e.g., Reddy and Iyer partnering to build one commercial building in Hyderabad, or two architects teaming up for one housing project).

General Partnership: The standard form governed by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. All partners have unlimited personal liability (joint and several), all may participate in management, and every partner can bind the firm in the ordinary course of business.

Limited Partnership: Has at least one general partner (unlimited liability) and at least one limited/ special partner (liability capped at invested capital; cannot manage or bind the firm). Not formally recognised under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932; its Indian equivalent is the Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) under the LLP Act, 2008.

modules.title: Rights and Duties of Partners (Sections 9–16, 36–37)
text: Some duties are absolute (cannot be changed by agreement), while most rights and other duties are default rules (apply unless the partnership deed states otherwise).

Participate in ManagementSection 12(a): Equal right to take part in conducting business. Ordinary matters decided by majority; changing the nature of business requires unanimous consent of all partners.
Access Books of AccountsSection 12(d): Unconditional right of every partner to inspect and copy firm books at any time (cannot be excluded by agreement).

Share in ProfitsSection 13(b): Equal share in profits and equal contribution to losses unless deed states otherwise. (Note: Under S.13(a), no partner is entitled to remuneration for managing unless agreed.)

Interest on Capital & AdvancesSections 13(c) & 13(d): Interest on capital is paid ONLY if agreed in deed and ONLY out of profits. Any advance beyond agreed capital earns 6% per annum interest regardless of profit (e.g., Priya in Chennai advancing Rs 5 lakh earns 6% p.a. even with zero profit).

Right to IndemnitySection 13(e): Firm must compensate a partner for payments/ liabilities incurred in ordinary business or in an emergency to protect the firm from loss (acting with ordinary prudence).
Share Firm PropertySection 14: Firm property is held jointly strictly for business purposes; no partner owns a specific asset individually.

Rights of an Outgoing PartnerSections 36 & 37: Right to settlement of capital, profits, and goodwill on exit. If the firm keeps using the outgoing partner's unsettled share, they can claim profit attributable to that share OR 6% p.a. interest, whichever is higher.
Carry on Business to Greatest Common AdvantageSection 9: Absolute duty (cannot be waived): act in the firm's best interest, not personal gain.
Good Faith & Utmost FidelitySection 9: Absolute fiduciary duty: be honest, disclose material facts, avoid conflicts of interest.
Render True Accounts & Full InformationSection 9: Absolute duty: provide true accounts and complete information to any partner or their legal representative.
Indemnify for FraudSection 10: Absolute duty: compensate the firm for any loss caused by the partner's fraud or wilful misrepresentation.
Attend DiligentlySection 12(b): Attend duties carefully; wilful neglect causing loss makes the partner liable to indemnify the firm (Section 13(f)).
Not to Make Personal/Secret ProfitSection 16(a): Must account for and pay to the firm any personal profit made from firm transactions, property, name, or connections.

Not to Compete with the FirmSection 16(b): If a partner runs a competing business without consent, they must hand over all profits earned from it to the firm (e.g., Ramesh in Ahmedabad secretly running a rival trading firm).
Note: Serious breaches (fraud, concealment, persistent neglect) can lead to dissolution by court order under Section 44.

modules.title: Dissolution of a Firm (Sections 40–44)
text: Dissolution of a Firm: Means completely winding up the firm and ending the partnership relationship among ALL partners.

Distinction: Dissolution of Partnership (e.g., Retirement) only changes the relationship while remaining partners continue the firm; Dissolution of a Firm ends the entire business and starts winding up.
By ConsentSection 40: At any time with the consent of all partners.
By AgreementSection 40: In accordance with an existing contract or provision in the partnership deed.
Contingent DissolutionSection 42: On expiry of a fixed term, completion of a specific venture, death of a partner, or insolvency of a partner (unless the deed provides otherwise).
By NoticeSection 43: In a partnership at will, any partner can dissolve the firm by giving written notice to all other partners.

By the CourtSection 44: On a partner's lawsuit due to insanity, permanent incapacity, misconduct, persistent breach of agreement, transfer of interest, perpetual losses, or any other just and equitable ground.

modules.title: Minor as a Partner (Section 30)
text: Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a minor (below 18 years; or 21 years if a court- appointed guardian exists) cannot contract—any contract with a minor is void ab initio. Therefore, a minor CANNOT become a full partner or start a new partnership. Exception (Section 30): With the consent of ALL existing adult partners, a minor may be admitted to the BENEFITS of an already existing partnership.

Example: Vinod and Kavita admit Vinod's 14-year-old son Aryan to the benefits of their manufacturing firm. Aryan shares profits and can inspect accounts, but has no personal liability for losses and is not a party to the deed.

Right to Share in Profits — Entitled to the agreed share of firm profits.: No Personal Liability for Losses — Only the minor's share in firm property is liable; personal assets are completely protected.
Right to Inspect & Copy Accounts — Minor or guardian can check books to verify profit share.: No Right to Participate in Management — Admitted only to financial benefits, not governance.

Right to Share in Firm's Property — Entitled to agreed share of net assets on dissolution.: Cannot Sue Partners for Full Account — Cannot sue for dissolution or a full partnership account like an adult partner.

Right to Sue for Their Share — Can sue partners if agreed profit/property share is not paid (but not over management).: Cannot Bind the Firm — Has no authority to act as agent or sign contracts binding other partners.
Within 6 months of turning 18 (or 6 months of learning they were admitted to benefits, whichever is later), the person must decide and give public notice:

No Action Taken (Deemed Continuation – Section 30(6)): If no public notice is given within 6 months, the person automatically becomes a full partner with unlimited liability for both past and future debts.
